Then Shah-Arman, when he saw the eagerness of Saladin's men for battle,
and the faintheartedness of those who were with him,
said to the lord of Mosul and of Mardin:
"Henceforth it is the winter season,
and it is not suitable for fighting.
Rather, let everyone return to his own country,
and toward the spring let us assemble again."
And so they dispersed,
and their empty gathering was dissolved.
And Saladin sent and informed the Caliph of what the people of Mosul had done,
and that it was they who provoked him every time,
and not he them.
And he again received permission from the Caliph to wage war against Amid.
And in the year five hundred and seventy-nine
[579] of the Arabs, in the first month,
that is in the month of Iyyar of the year one thousand four hundred and ninety-four
[1494] of the Greeks,
Saladin captured Amid,
after he had pressed it hard in battle.
Now at that time Ibn Nisan the chief was ruling in Amid,
and he fought very valiantly against the besiegers outside.
However, the citizens turned their faces against him,
for the reason that on one occasion when Saladin's men entered between the two walls of Amid,
the citizens of Amid went out,
shut them all in there,
and killed them.
Then the Sultan wrote on arrows harsh threats, along with strong oaths,
that he would not turn away from it until he took it,
and then he would burn them all with fire,
unless they surrendered.
And when the people within feared this, and lost heart, and surrendered (literally: gave their hand),
Ibn Nisan also trembled,
and he obtained terms for his life, his household, and his possessions.
Then the Sultan permitted him
to carry out for three days whatever he wished from his residence.
And in this way he surrendered the city,
and the Sultan entered.
And Ibn Nisan began to bring out for three days from his courts gold, silver, precious stones, and vessels.
And it is said
that he was not able to bring out even one tenth of his property in the three days,
because he had amassed a vast wealth in Amid.
And when Saladin captured Amid,
he gave it to Nur al-Din, son of Qara Arslan, with everything that was in it.
Now certain people said to Saladin:
"You promised him the city,
and not everything that is in it,
this immense treasure which is worth more than three millions of dinars!"
